hero.headline: Oil Prices Drop as U.S.-Iran Agreement to Reopen Strait of Hormuz Takes Effect
hero.body:
Oil prices fell sharply after President Trump confirmed a U.S.-Iran peace deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker traffic. The agreement marks a turning point following more than 100 days of disruption to global energy supplies, with Brent crude tumbling to $82 a barrel and wholesale gas prices dropping around 6 percent.

The strait, which handles roughly 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied gas during normal times, had been closed as the conflict between the U.S. and Iran intensified. The blockade created one of the most severe disruptions to energy markets on record, driving fuel costs upward worldwide and creating shortages across multiple industries.

Financial markets reacted positively to the news. Stock indices climbed as investors welcomed the prospect of stabilized energy supplies returning to global markets. The Nasdaq prepared to rebound, while major indices including the Dow and S&P 500 posted gains. Analysts noted that optimism around the Iran deal helped offset concerns about hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve.

American consumers saw immediate relief at the pump. Gasoline prices fell below four dollars per gallon for the first time in months, representing a significant decline from the elevated costs that followed the conflict's start in February. The drop came as supply fears eased with the strait's reopening to tanker traffic.

The reopening also had broader diplomatic effects. Britain dropped its "do not travel" advisory for Dubai, where thousands of British travelers had been stranded when the conflict erupted. The Bank of England held interest rates steady, maintaining its December rate cut as the central bank continued monitoring the impact of high energy prices on the economy.

However, analysts cautioned that full recovery would take time. Energy markets noted that oil and gas prices were unlikely to return to pre-war levels for months, as buyers rushed to refill depleted emergency crude stockpiles. About 20,000 seafarers and 2,000 ships remained stranded in the Gulf, according to the International Maritime Organization, though the reopening should eventually clear these backlogs.

The economic toll of the disruption had spread globally. Germany, Europe's largest economy, halved its 2026 growth forecast to 0.5 percent, while Greece announced 500 million euros in extra aid for households and farmers facing elevated costs for fuel and other essential goods.

Asian markets prepared for mixed trading as investors weighed the positive supply news against lingering uncertainty around Federal Reserve policy and longer-term economic impacts from the extended energy crisis. The reopening of the strait represented a significant diplomatic and economic milestone, though full normalcy in global energy markets remained months away.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rules government cannot bar gun ownership based on marijuana use
cards.body:
The Supreme Court issued a unanimous decision stating that the federal government cannot restrict gun ownership based on marijuana use alone. The ruling came in a case involving a Texas man named Ali Danial Hemani who was prosecuted under a federal law that prohibits people classified as habitual drug users from possessing firearms.

The justices determined that the law violated Hemani's Second Amendment right to bear arms and found the statute to be unconstitutionally vague. The rare unanimous decision demonstrates broad agreement across the ideological spectrum on this constitutional issue.

Federal law has long contained a blanket prohibition on firearm possession by individuals deemed habitual drug users. This restriction has been applied to marijuana consumers regardless of whether they live in states where the drug is legal for medical or recreational purposes. The government argued that maintaining this restriction served legitimate public safety interests, but the court rejected this rationale.

The unanimous nature of the ruling suggests the justices identified fundamental constitutional problems with the law that transcended typical partisan disagreements on gun policy. This consensus across a divided court indicates concern about how the statute's language and application may infringe on constitutional protections.

The decision carries significant implications for federal firearms law enforcement. More than half of American states have legalized marijuana for medical use, and roughly two dozen states allow recreational use. However, the federal government continues to classify marijuana as a Schedule I controlled substance, creating a conflict between state and federal policy.

The court's ruling may force federal lawmakers to reconsider how gun restrictions interact with changing state marijuana laws. States that have legalized the drug now face questions about how to harmonize their policies with federal firearms regulations. The decision could affect numerous individuals across the country who use marijuana legally under state law but remain subject to federal gun restrictions.

The full implications of this ruling will become clearer as the court issues its complete written opinion and lower courts apply the precedent in future cases. The decision addresses a growing tension in American law as state-level marijuana reforms continue expanding while federal prohibitions remain in place.

This case represents a notable moment in the evolution of gun rights jurisprudence. It shows the court willing to strike down federal restrictions on firearm ownership even when tied to drug policy concerns. The ruling underscores how changing social attitudes and state laws around marijuana are forcing reconsideration of longstanding federal restrictions that were established when marijuana prohibitions faced virtually no state-level challenge.

cards.headline: Ukraine Launches Largest Drone Attack on Moscow Since War Began
cards.body:
Ukraine deployed nearly 200 drones in a massive assault on Moscow on Thursday, marking the largest aerial strike on the Russian capital since the war's full-scale invasion began. The attack set a major oil refinery ablaze and temporarily forced evacuations at Russia's largest airport.

The primary target was the Kapotnya oil refinery in Moscow's southeastern district, a facility that supplies approximately 40 percent of the capital's petrol and roughly half of its diesel fuel. Video footage captured a fuel tank detonating explosively, with flames consuming one of Moscow's most critical energy infrastructure sites. Beyond the refinery, Ukrainian drones struck a shopping center, residential buildings, industrial facilities and private homes. Russian authorities reported at least 17 people injured in the strikes.

The scale of this attack suggests Ukraine has significantly strained Moscow's air defense systems, which are the densest in Russia. Online videos showed Ukrainian drones flying over the capital with minimal interception, indicating some weapons successfully penetrated the layered defenses. Footage also captured Russian operators attempting last-minute countermeasures, including one soldier firing a shoulder-launched missile moments before a drone hit the refinery.

Ukraine appears to have employed a mix of conventional propeller-driven long-range drones alongside newer jet-powered missile systems. These faster, harder-to-intercept weapons, including the recently unveiled Bars hybrid drone-cruise missile, pose growing challenges for Russian air defenses. Moscow faces constraints in deploying its defensive systems in densely populated areas, where interceptor misses or falling debris could cause significant civilian casualties.

Residents in areas east of Moscow reported an unusual phenomenon following the refinery strike. Black rain, an oily residue from the burning refinery, coated cars, streets and buildings. This visual evidence brought the war directly to Moscow residents in unprecedented ways. Russian social media filled with videos of Muscovites reacting to the strikes, with some residents describing shaking windows and smoke-darkened skies.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy framed the attack as retaliation for Russia's earlier strike on a historic Kyiv monastery. "If Ukraine is going to burn, your Moscow will burn too," he stated in a voice message. "It is time to end the aggression, time to end this war."

The refinery damage could significantly affect fuel supplies throughout the Moscow region, though Russia may redirect supplies from other sources. Beyond the immediate practical consequences, the strike's psychological impact proved substantial. For the first time in years of conflict, Moscow's residents directly witnessed the war's consequences, with smoke visible from apartment windows and the air thick with the smell of burning fuel.

Russian officials have not yet formally responded. However, nationalist figures demanded retaliation, with some calling for escalated responses. Historical patterns suggest Moscow will likely answer with renewed waves of missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities.

cards.headline: U.S. Unemployment Claims Fall to 226,000 in Sign of Labor Market Strength
cards.teaser: Weekly jobless claims dropped, indicating that layoffs remain at historically low levels despite economic uncertainty.
cards.body:
U.S. jobless claims dropped to 226,000 last week, continuing a trend of strong labor market performance. The decline reflects sustained employer restraint on layoffs, keeping dismissals near historic lows.

The data demonstrates resilience in American employment despite headwinds elsewhere in the economy. Employers continue retaining workers, suggesting confidence in ongoing business conditions.

cards.headline: Stock Markets Advance Despite Hawkish Federal Reserve Signals
cards.teaser: Major U.S. stock indices climbed as optimism over the Iran deal offset concerns about the Federal Reserve's monetary policy direction.
cards.body:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at 3.5% to 3.75%, where they have remained since December. However, the central bank signaled a possible rate hike before year's end under new chair Kevin Warsh. The Fed's voting committee unanimously supported the decision, noting that economic activity is expanding at a solid pace.

US stock markets declined on Wednesday afternoon following the Fed's hawkish signals. Investors are now weighing the prospect of higher borrowing costs ahead as the year progresses.

cards.headline: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh Opts Against Policy Guidance at First Meeting
cards.teaser: New Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to provide forward guidance on monetary policy, prompting investors to increase bets on higher interest rates.
cards.body:
Kevin Warsh held US interest rates steady between 3.5% and 3.75% at his first meeting as Federal Reserve chairman. Rather than providing forward guidance on future policy decisions, Warsh plans to review how the Fed operates.

The decision to withhold policy signals represents a shift from recent communication practices, leaving investors uncertain about the central bank's next moves on interest rates.

cards.headline: Senate committee advances bipartisan college sports regulation bill
cards.teaser: The Protect College Sports Act passed 19-9 and moves to the full Senate.
cards.body:
The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee advanced the Protect College Sports Act in a 19-9 vote, sending the bipartisan measure to regulate college sports to the Senate floor. Twelve Republicans and seven Democrats supported the bill, while seven Democrats and two Republicans opposed it.

Sens. Roger Wicker of Mississippi and others voted against the measure. The bill seeks to establish federal regulations for college athletics. The committee's approval marks a step toward potential nationwide standards for collegiate sports governance.

cards.headline: Vice President Vance Defends US-Iran Agreement as Critics Question War's Purpose
cards.teaser: The vice president said Iran's nuclear program has been destroyed and its capacity to threaten neighbors is largely gone.
cards.body:
Vice President Vance defended the Iran agreement, stating that the country's nuclear program has been completely destroyed and its capacity to threaten its neighbors is largely gone. According to Vance, Iran will only receive economic benefits if its leaders change their behavior. The agreement was signed to end the war and open the Strait of Hormuz.

The deal has drawn significant criticism from analysts and observers who question the war's overall purpose and outcome. While acknowledging the human cost, critics argue that the Iranian regime has not only survived but has emerged stronger from the conflict. The agreement has also coincided with the president's approval rating hitting record lows.

cards.headline: Israeli Foreign Minister Cuts Off Contact With EU Diplomat
cards.teaser: The move follows reported remarks by the EU foreign policy chief comparing Israeli actions to apartheid.
cards.body:
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced he is severing all contact with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. The decision came after Kallas allegedly made comparisons between Israeli policies and apartheid, which Sa'ar characterized as a blood libel.

Kallas has called for dialogue following the Israeli announcement. The dispute threatens to deepen divisions in EU-Israel relations and creates a foreign policy crisis within European diplomatic circles at a time of heightened tensions in the region.

cards.headline: Iran Emerges From War Stronger Than Expected, Analysis Finds
cards.teaser: The Iranian regime survived military action and may be better positioned than many analysts predicted.
cards.body:
Iran has emerged from the first chapter of the conflict stronger than many observers anticipated, according to BBC Persian Service analysis. Rather than being weakened, the Iranian regime has been empowered by the outcome.

The development raises questions about the war's strategic purpose. Iran now confronts a different set of challenges moving forward, which may prove more difficult to manage than the direct military threats it faced during the conflict.

cards.headline: Archbishop of Canterbury Apologizes for Forced Adoptions by Church of England
cards.teaser: Tens of thousands of babies were taken from unmarried women and girls from the 1950s to the 1980s.
cards.body:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has apologized for the Church of England's involvement in forced adoptions spanning the 1950s through 1980s. Tens of thousands of babies were taken from unmarried women and girls during this period, when unwed pregnancy carried severe social stigma.

The church acknowledged the profound suffering caused by these institutional policies, recognizing the pain, shame and indignity experienced by affected families who were separated from their children.

cards.headline: Israel Questions Strategy After US-Iran Agreement
cards.teaser: The deal accomplishes none of Israel's stated war aims, according to analysts.
cards.body:
Israeli officials view the US-Iran agreement as a strategic setback. The deal fails to achieve Israel's stated war objectives and leaves the country in a weakened position across its core security concerns.

The agreement has prompted Israeli leaders to reassess their approach. Meanwhile, observers note that Iran has emerged from the conflict stronger than anticipated, having not only survived the war but gained additional leverage through the diplomatic settlement.

cards.headline: Jury Fails to Reach Verdict in Norwegian Trial
cards.teaser: A 19-year-old defendant was remanded in custody and will face a retrial.
cards.body:
A jury in Norway was unable to reach a verdict in the trial of Johannes Natland, 19. The court remanded Natland in custody following the hung jury.

The case will now proceed to a retrial. Norwegian legal procedure requires a new jury to hear the case when the initial panel cannot reach a unanimous or sufficient majority decision.

hero.headline: Supreme Court limits federal law barring drug users from gun ownership
hero.body:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of a Texas man who challenged a federal law prohibiting drug users from possessing firearms, finding the statute violated the Second Amendment and was unconstitutionally vague. The decision marks another expansion of gun rights under the current court and limits the federal government's power to disarm individuals based on drug use.

The case centered on a Texas marijuana user who was prosecuted under the federal law after attempting to purchase a firearm. His attorneys argued that the prohibition infringed on his constitutional right to bear arms. The court agreed, determining that the law as applied in this case could not withstand Second Amendment scrutiny.

The ruling narrows the scope of federal firearms restrictions, building on recent Supreme Court decisions that have expanded gun rights. Legal experts note the decision could affect how federal authorities enforce existing gun laws, particularly in states where marijuana use has been legalized or decriminalized. The court found the statute's language too vague to provide clear guidance on who qualifies as a prohibited drug user.

The decision has significant implications for the intersection of drug policy and gun rights. With marijuana legal for recreational or medical use in many states but still prohibited federally, the ruling creates questions about how firearms laws will be enforced going forward. Federal authorities have historically used drug use as grounds to deny gun purchases or prosecute illegal possession.

The case represents the latest in a series of Supreme Court rulings that have strengthened Second Amendment protections. The court's majority has consistently ruled that federal and state governments must meet a high standard to justify restrictions on gun ownership. Civil liberties groups on both sides of the gun debate are analyzing the decision's potential reach, as it could affect other categories of people currently barred from firearm possession under federal law.

cards.headline: Algae bloom covers Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after $14 million renovation
cards.teaser: The Reflecting Pool has experienced one of the largest algae blooms in years, weeks after a $14 million renovation was completed.
cards.body:
The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington has been overtaken by a major algae bloom, one of the biggest recorded in recent years. The green water comes shortly after the completion of a $14 million renovation project intended to improve the monument's appearance and infrastructure.

Aerial photographs show the pool covered in green algae, prompting the Trump administration to label the cleanup a regional and national priority ahead of July 4 celebrations.

cards.headline: Teen dies after fall from horse-drawn carriage in Central Park
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old tourist died after being thrown from a horse-drawn carriage near a popular New York City destination.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old died after being thrown from a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park on Wednesday afternoon. The incident occurred when the carriage horse bolted and the vehicle tipped over. At least two passengers were ejected from the carriage during the accident.

The horse bolted after the carriage driver stepped down to photograph the passengers. The teenager was one of four people riding in the carriage at the time. Horse-drawn carriages remain a popular tourist attraction in Central Park, though they have faced ongoing criticism regarding safety and animal welfare concerns.

cards.headline: Three brothers navigate life after parents' deaths from loss of HIV medication access
cards.teaser: A 17-year-old heads his family after his parents died following loss of access to HIV medications, leaving three brothers to care for themselves.
cards.body:
Three brothers in the United States are managing a household on their own after their mother and father died from complications related to losing access to their HIV medications. The oldest brother, now 17, has become the head of the family, facing challenges including tight finances and a leaking roof.

The boys are working to navigate daily life without parents while dealing with the aftermath of their deaths. Their situation highlights ongoing issues around medication access and the consequences when treatment for chronic conditions is interrupted. The family is figuring out how to manage basic needs and maintain stability in the face of their loss.

cards.headline: UK drops 'do not travel' warning for Dubai
cards.teaser: Britain has lifted its travel warning for Dubai months after thousands of British citizens were stranded when the US-Iran war began.
cards.body:
The United Kingdom has lifted its 'do not travel' advisory for Dubai. The warning had been in place since early 2026 when conflict between the US and Iran erupted, leaving thousands of British travelers stranded in the Middle East.

With the situation now improved, British authorities have determined it is safe enough to allow travel to the popular tourism and business destination to resume.

cards.headline: Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russian oil infrastructure near Moscow
cards.teaser: Nearly 200 Ukrainian drones struck targets southeast of the Russian capital, causing fires at a refinery and shopping center.
cards.body:
Ukrainian forces conducted their largest air raid on Moscow since the invasion began, deploying nearly 200 drones against targets southeast of the capital. The strikes ignited a major oil refinery and a shopping center, with residents reporting black rain falling across the city in the aftermath.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy characterized the attack as retaliation for Russia's earlier strike on a historic monastery complex in Kyiv. The operation also forced evacuations at Russia's largest airport. Zelenskyy stated: "If Ukraine is going to burn, your Moscow will burn too," calling for an end to the war.

cards.headline: Harry Kane equals Gary Lineker's England World Cup goal record
cards.teaser: England captain Harry Kane scored his 10th World Cup goal, matching Gary Lineker's national record.
cards.body:
Harry Kane has equaled Gary Lineker's record of 10 World Cup goals for England. Following the achievement, Lineker praised Kane, describing him as "the greatest English striker we've ever had."

Kane's milestone underscores his prominence in English football history, matching one of the country's most celebrated former players in this particular measure of World Cup success.

cards.headline: Apple to Raise Prices as AI Boom Drives Up Memory Chip Costs
cards.teaser: Apple announced plans to increase prices due to rising costs of memory chips driven by artificial intelligence demand.
cards.body:
Apple's outgoing CEO Tim Cook has announced that the company plans to raise prices in response to surging demand for memory chips from the artificial intelligence sector. The shortage of advanced chips is creating pricing pressure across the technology industry as manufacturers compete for limited supply.

Cook did not specify which products would see price increases or when they would take effect. The moves reflect how AI's rapid growth is reshaping cost structures for major tech companies dealing with constrained chip availability.

cards.headline: SpaceX Stock Declines After Three-Day Rally Following IPO
cards.teaser: SpaceX shares fell six percent in their first decline since the company's historic initial public offering.
cards.body:
SpaceX stock dropped after breaking a three-day winning streak that followed the company's market debut. The shares slid five to six percent despite analysts issuing major price target increases for the newly public space company.

The decline came as a rival company won a NASA contract for a Mars mission. Financial advisers cautioned potential investors about factors to consider before purchasing SpaceX stock. The IPO had created overnight millionaires among SpaceX employees, including a former welder whose stake became worth over one million dollars.

cards.headline: U.S. Unemployment Claims Fall to 226,000 in Sign of Labor Market Strength
cards.teaser: Weekly jobless claims dropped, indicating that layoffs remain at historically low levels despite economic uncertainty.
cards.body:
U.S. jobless claims dropped to 226,000 last week, continuing a trend of strong labor market performance. The decline reflects sustained employer restraint on layoffs, keeping dismissals near historic lows.

The data demonstrates resilience in American employment despite headwinds elsewhere in the economy. Employers continue retaining workers, suggesting confidence in ongoing business conditions.

cards.headline: Bank of England Holds Interest Rates Amid Energy Price Concerns
cards.teaser: The Bank of England kept interest rates unchanged, citing the impact of elevated energy prices on the economy.
cards.body:
The Bank of England held interest rates steady, citing ongoing uncertainty from Middle East upheaval. The central bank last reduced rates in December but has paused further cuts as energy market volatility continues to concern policymakers assessing the economic impact.

The decision reflects broader economic pressures on UK households and businesses. Retail sales growth has slowed significantly, with major chains reporting that geopolitical uncertainty is affecting consumer spending and confidence.

hero.headline: Waymo recalls nearly 4,000 robotaxis after vehicles entered construction zones
hero.body:
Waymo has issued a recall affecting nearly 4,000 of its autonomous vehicles after the company identified multiple instances where its robotaxis drove into highway sections that were closed for construction. The recall addresses a software issue that allowed the vehicles to navigate into restricted areas meant for construction workers and equipment.

The company has documented at least 13 separate occasions where its self-driving vehicles entered highway construction zones. The incidents raised safety concerns about the ability of the autonomous driving system to properly recognize and respond to temporary road closures and construction barriers. Waymo operates one of the largest commercial robotaxi fleets in the United States, providing rides to passengers in several cities.

The recall involves a software update to correct the navigation system that failed to properly identify and avoid construction zones. Waymo will deploy the fix to its fleet to prevent the vehicles from entering areas where active construction work is taking place. The nature of the software issue means the company can address the problem through remote updates rather than requiring physical modifications to the vehicles.

The construction zone incidents highlight ongoing challenges in autonomous vehicle technology, particularly in handling dynamic road conditions that change frequently. Construction zones present unique obstacles for self-driving systems because they often involve temporary signage, modified traffic patterns, and barriers that may not appear in standard mapping data. These environments require vehicles to process and respond to visual cues that differ from normal driving conditions.

Waymo has been expanding its robotaxi operations across multiple markets as it works to demonstrate the safety and reliability of autonomous vehicles for commercial passenger service. The recall comes as regulators and the public continue to scrutinize the safety record of self-driving vehicles operating on public roads. The company has not disclosed whether any collisions or injuries resulted from the vehicles entering the construction zones.

cards.headline: Apple opens App Store to new competition in Brazil
cards.teaser: Apple is allowing alternative app distribution methods on iPhones in Brazil, loosening its control over how users download software.
cards.body:
Apple has begun opening up iPhone app distribution in Brazil, marking another major market where the company is reducing its exclusive control over how users obtain software. The change allows for new competition in app distribution beyond the official App Store.

Brazil joins other regions where Apple has been required to permit alternative app marketplaces and payment systems on its devices. The shift represents a significant change to Apple's business model in one of Latin America's largest technology markets.

cards.headline: AI startup General Intuition in talks to raise $300 million
cards.teaser: General Intuition is negotiating a funding round of around $300 million at roughly $2 billion valuation with backers including Jeff Bezos.
cards.body:
General Intuition is raising approximately $300 million in funding at a valuation around $2 billion. Jeff Bezos is among the backers participating in the investment round.

The startup specializes in training AI agents focused on spatial-temporal reasoning—technology designed to understand how objects and events relate to each other across physical space and time.

cards.headline: Adobe adds AI assistant to Premiere, Illustrator and InDesign
cards.teaser: Adobe is expanding its Firefly AI assistant with new capabilities and integrating it into Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign and Frame.io.
cards.body:
Adobe is expanding its Firefly AI assistant across its creative suite, adding the tool to Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, and Frame.io. The updates give the AI assistant new capabilities while integrating it deeper into Adobe's core creative applications.

The rollout brings AI-powered features directly into the workflows of video editors, designers, and publishers who rely on these industry-standard tools for their work.

cards.headline: Former cosmonaut Aleksandr Samokutyaev dies at 56
cards.teaser: Aleksandr Samokutyaev, who flew two missions to the International Space Station, has died at age 56.
cards.body:
Aleksandr Samokutyaev, a Russian cosmonaut who served on the International Space Station, has died. He was 56 years old. Samokutyaev completed two expeditions to the ISS during his career with the space program.

During his time as a cosmonaut, Samokutyaev conducted two spacewalks and spent a total of 322 days in orbit. He becomes the first former ISS crew member to die, marking a notable moment in the history of the space station program that has hosted hundreds of astronauts and cosmonauts since operations began.

cards.headline: Spotify launches Reserved ticket system for concert superfans
cards.teaser: Spotify is rolling out Reserved, a new feature that holds two concert tickets for an artist's top listeners before public sales begin.
cards.body:
Spotify is rolling out Reserved, a new ticketing feature that gives the platform's biggest fans early access to concert tickets. The system reserves two tickets for superfans before general public sales begin, based on their listening history with specific artists.

Reserved allows Spotify to leverage its streaming data to identify devoted listeners and connect them directly with live events. This marks Spotify's entry into the concert ticketing market, creating a new benefit for engaged users on the platform.

cards.headline: Pixi app turns text messages into augmented reality experiences
cards.teaser: A new iOS app called Pixi transforms text messages into interactive augmented reality content instead of traditional stickers or emoji.
cards.body:
Pixi has launched an iOS app that transforms text messaging by embedding interactive augmented reality experiences directly into conversations. The application moves beyond traditional messaging enhancements like stickers, GIFs, and emoji reactions to introduce three-dimensional interactive elements into text threads.

The company views augmented reality as the next evolution in mobile communication, enabling users to create and share AR content within their messaging conversations.

hero.headline: Knicks celebrate first NBA championship since 1973 with parade in New York
hero.body:
The New York Knicks secured their first NBA title in over five decades with a stunning victory against the San Antonio Spurs in Game 4 of the Finals. The 107-106 win marked one of the most dramatic comebacks in basketball history.

Facing a 29-point deficit at one point during the game, the Knicks mounted an improbable rally to claim the championship. OG Anunoby's tip-in with 1.2 seconds remaining proved to be the decisive play. Jalen Brunson had missed a contested three-pointer in the closing moments, but Anunoby slipped through the defense to secure the victory.

"Right hand from God," said Knicks center Karl-Anthony Towns, describing Anunoby's winning basket.

The Spurs dominated most of the game. San Antonio buried 11 of their first 16 attempts from three-point range and held a 76-49 lead at halftime, marking the largest half-time advantage by a visiting team in NBA Finals history. The deficit reached 29 points with 9 minutes and 40 seconds remaining in the third quarter.

The Knicks' turnaround began in the third quarter when New York held San Antonio to just 14 points on 4-for-20 shooting. The fourth quarter brought an explosive 28-9 run over seven minutes as the team converted defensive stops into fast-break opportunities. Brunson delivered a key lay-up with 1 minute and 22 seconds left to give the Knicks their first lead of the game.

Anunoby finished with 33 points and made seven of nine attempts from beyond the arc, both playoff career highs. Brunson added 36 points and seven assists. Jose Alvarado provided crucial support off the bench with eight points during the fourth-quarter surge.

"You're down 29, you're thinking, 'OK let's get it to 20,'" said Josh Hart. "There's three minutes left in the third quarter, we're down 18, you're thinking, 'Let's get it to 10.' In the fourth quarter, you're like, 'This is winning time. Anything can happen.'"

Victor Wembanyama led San Antonio with 24 points and 13 rebounds, while Devin Harper contributed 21 points. The Spurs were outscored 58-30 in the second half and shot just 3-for-17 from three-point range after halftime.

The championship represents the franchise's first title since 1973 and the third in the team's 80-year history. No team had previously overcome a deficit greater than 24 points in an NBA Finals game. Only LeBron James's Cleveland Cavaliers in 2016 have overturned a 3-1 deficit to win the Finals.

The victory ended one of the longest title droughts in North American professional sports and sparked celebrations throughout New York City.

cards.headline: Fog delays opening round of U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills
cards.teaser: The first round of the U.S. Open was halted by fog before top players including Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler began their rounds.
cards.body:
Fog forced a delay to the opening round of the 2026 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills before play could begin. Players including Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler were scheduled for early tee times but had not started when fog halted proceedings.

The tournament marks a return to Shinnecock Hills. The USGA created opening round groupings featuring several notable pairings, including French players.

cards.headline: Raleigh prepares for Hurricanes Stanley Cup championship parade
cards.teaser: The city of Raleigh issued guidance for fans planning to attend the Carolina Hurricanes' Stanley Cup championship parade scheduled for Saturday.
cards.body:
Raleigh officials urged fans to carpool or use public transportation for the Hurricanes' Stanley Cup championship parade. The city released a guide for attendees as excitement builds throughout the region following the team's first Stanley Cup victory. The Stanley Cup has been on tour in Raleigh, further elevating enthusiasm among Hurricanes supporters.

ESPN analyzed how the Hurricanes assembled their championship roster through what they described as a collaboration between traditional hockey knowledge and analytical approaches. The victory represents the first Stanley Cup title in franchise history for the Carolina-based team.

cards.headline: Glenn Phillips scores first Test century for New Zealand against England
cards.teaser: New Zealand's Glenn Phillips reached his maiden Test century against England at The Oval, helping his team to 391 runs.
cards.body:
Glenn Phillips reached his first Test century for New Zealand against England at The Oval on the second day of the second Test. His innings proved crucial as New Zealand compiled a first-innings total of 391 runs, with Phillips leading the charge throughout their batting effort.

England began their reply, with Ben Duckett dismissed for 36 in a run-out, leaving the hosts at 45-1 as they looked to respond to New Zealand's substantial score.

cards.headline: Ben Stokes named in Durham squad after being dropped from England captaincy
cards.teaser: Ben Stokes will return to county cricket for Durham in their match against Northamptonshire after losing the England captaincy.
cards.body:
Ben Stokes will return to action for Durham in their County Championship match against Northamptonshire on Friday. The all-rounder has been named in the squad following his removal from the England Test captaincy.

This will be Stokes' first competitive appearance since stepping down from the leadership role.

cards.headline: Ivory Coast striker Elye Wahi denied entry to Canada for World Cup
cards.teaser: Ivory Coast forward Elye Wahi was refused entry into Canada at the World Cup amid an ongoing betting investigation.
cards.body:
Elye Wahi, an Ivory Coast striker, has been denied entry to Canada for his team's World Cup match against Germany in Toronto on Saturday. The Ivory Coast football federation confirmed that the necessary administrative authorisations for his entry into Canadian territory could not be obtained.

Wahi is currently under investigation for alleged match-fixing in Ligue 1, which appears to have affected his ability to enter Canada for the tournament.

cards.headline: Fox World Cup pundits Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Alexi Lalas clash on air
cards.teaser: Former stars Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Alexi Lalas engaged in heated exchanges during Fox's World Cup coverage, sparking viewer attention.
cards.body:
Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Alexi Lalas, both serving as analysts for Fox's World Cup broadcasts, clashed on live television during tournament coverage. Ibrahimovic criticized Lalas in exchanges that multiple outlets described as contentious, with one report characterizing Ibrahimovic's comments as calling Lalas ignorant. The on-air tension between the two former international players drew significant attention on social media.

Separately, Thierry Henry took issue with U.S. analyst Landon Donovan's characterization of France as arrogant during coverage of France's opening match. The exchanges highlight tensions among the international panel Fox assembled for its World Cup broadcasts.

hero.headline: Jay Leno Says Joe Rogan Has Become the New Johnny Carson
hero.body:
Former Tonight Show host Jay Leno compared podcaster Joe Rogan to legendary late-night television host Johnny Carson, suggesting that Rogan now occupies the cultural position Carson once held. Leno made this observation while reflecting on how entertainment and media have transformed over the decades.

"Joe talks to everybody about everything," Leno said, drawing a parallel between Rogan's interview approach and Carson's talent for engaging with a wide variety of guests during his time hosting The Tonight Show. Carson hosted the program from 1962 to 1992 and became one of the most influential figures in American television history.

Rogan hosts The Joe Rogan Experience, currently the biggest podcast in the United States by most metrics. He conducts lengthy conversations with guests including comedians, athletes, scientists, and politicians. The podcast moved to Spotify in 2020 under an exclusive licensing deal reportedly worth over 100 million dollars. His episodes typically run two to three hours, a significant difference from the structured time segments of traditional late-night television.

The comparison highlights a shift in how Americans consume entertainment and information. While Carson built a massive television audience during an era when viewing options were limited, Rogan has developed an equally influential platform in today's fragmented digital media landscape. Both figures became known for their ability to conduct extended, relatively informal conversations with guests that appealed to audiences across demographic and political lines.

Leno succeeded Carson as Tonight Show host in 1992, holding the position until 2009 and again from 2010 to 2014. His remarks acknowledge that the cultural center of conversational entertainment has moved from broadcast television to digital platforms, where Rogan's podcast reaches millions of listeners per episode without the restrictions of network standards or time slot limitations.

Political observers closely track Rogan's influence because his enormous listenership makes him a significant power broker for the digital age. His publicly stated voting decisions, including voting for Bernie Sanders in 2020 and Donald Trump in 2024, are considered as significant as traditional political endorsements. Rogan represents what some have called "America's most famous swing voter" because his views do not align neatly with either major political party. His shifting positions often signal broader changes in how politically fluid Americans are thinking about major issues.

Several prominent male comedy and talk-show podcasters who previously supported Trump have recently walked back their endorsements, including Rogan, Theo Von, and Andrew Schulz. Trump's immigration policies have particularly driven this reconsideration among these influential media figures, suggesting that Rogan's cultural position continues to reflect and potentially shape the perspectives of millions of listeners.

cards.headline: Tierra Whack Releases Two New Singles Ahead of Upcoming Album
cards.teaser: The rapper released "Totem" and "Wax Paper" as pre-release tracks from her forthcoming album.
cards.body:
Rapper Tierra Whack has released two new singles, "Totem" and "Wax Paper," from her forthcoming album Whack's Museum. The tracks directly address critics and doubters, showcasing her artistic talent and range as a musician.

Both singles are now available ahead of the full album release.

cards.headline: Polymarket Launches Weekly Podcast With Dear Media
cards.teaser: The prediction market platform is entering podcasting with a show blending celebrity news and real-time prediction data.
cards.body:
Polymarket has partnered with Dear Media to launch What Are the Odds?, a weekly podcast that combines celebrity news, internet trends, and prediction market data. The show features rotating hosts from Dear Media's network of popular programs.

The podcast marks Polymarket's move into entertainment content beyond its core prediction market business. Hosts include Claudia and Jackie Oshry from The Toast, alongside other personalities from Dear Media's roster.

cards.headline: Fox Secures Higher Ad Commitments Despite Weaker Upfront Market
cards.teaser: The network increased its upfront ad sales compared to last year, bucking industry trends.
cards.body:
Fox Corp. increased its upfront advertising commitments compared to the previous year, bucking industry trends. While Madison Avenue faces tighter budgets overall, Fox managed to grow its ad sales across sports, news, and entertainment properties.

The network's success in a weakened market stems largely from its robust sports programming portfolio. This content differentiates Fox from traditional cable offerings and continues to attract advertiser investment despite broader economic pressures on television's annual upfront sales cycle.

cards.headline: Midland Discusses Texas Influences on New Album
cards.teaser: The country band released their new album "Stages" featuring traditional country sounds.
cards.body:
Country band Midland released their new album titled Stages, positioning themselves as early adopters of neotraditional country sounds. The album arrives as traditional country styles and Urban Cowboy aesthetics have gained wider popularity in the genre.

The band discussed their long-standing commitment to Texas-influenced country music, which has now become more mainstream. Midland's approach predates the recent wave of artists embracing similar sounds.

cards.headline: Esports World Cup Documentary Returns to Prime Video
cards.teaser: The second season of the docuseries covering the competition for $70 million in prizes drops in late June.
cards.body:
Esports World Cup: Level Up returns for its second season on Prime Video on June 26, with all five episodes available simultaneously. The docuseries, directed by acclaimed filmmaker R.J. Cutler, follows competitors at the 2025 Esports World Cup as they compete for $70 million in total prize money.

Cutler, known for directing Martha on Netflix and Billie Eilish: The World's a Little Blurry for Apple TV, brings his storytelling expertise to explore the personal journeys of professional gamers competing at the highest level of esports.

cards.headline: Charles Band Horror Film Debuts on ReelShort Platform
cards.teaser: "Models vs. Werewolves" will premiere in vertical video format on the microdrama platform.
cards.body:
Models vs. Werewolves, a new horror film from director Charles Band and production banner Full Moon Artists, will debut on microdrama platform ReelShort in vertical video format. The film stars Dee Wallace and follows five models who retreat to a remote Airbnb during a rare full moon event.

The full moon event in the film occurs once every 500 years. The vertical format represents an adaptation of traditional filmmaking for mobile-focused viewing platforms.

hero.headline: Supreme Court rules government cannot bar gun ownership based on marijuana use
hero.body:
The Supreme Court issued a unanimous decision stating that the federal government cannot restrict gun ownership based on marijuana use alone. The ruling came in a case involving a Texas man named Ali Danial Hemani who was prosecuted under a federal law that prohibits people classified as habitual drug users from possessing firearms.

The justices determined that the law violated Hemani's Second Amendment right to bear arms and found the statute to be unconstitutionally vague. The rare unanimous decision demonstrates broad agreement across the ideological spectrum on this constitutional issue.

Federal law has long contained a blanket prohibition on firearm possession by individuals deemed habitual drug users. This restriction has been applied to marijuana consumers regardless of whether they live in states where the drug is legal for medical or recreational purposes. The government argued that maintaining this restriction served legitimate public safety interests, but the court rejected this rationale.

The unanimous nature of the ruling suggests the justices identified fundamental constitutional problems with the law that transcended typical partisan disagreements on gun policy. This consensus across a divided court indicates concern about how the statute's language and application may infringe on constitutional protections.

The decision carries significant implications for federal firearms law enforcement. More than half of American states have legalized marijuana for medical use, and roughly two dozen states allow recreational use. However, the federal government continues to classify marijuana as a Schedule I controlled substance, creating a conflict between state and federal policy.

The court's ruling may force federal lawmakers to reconsider how gun restrictions interact with changing state marijuana laws. States that have legalized the drug now face questions about how to harmonize their policies with federal firearms regulations. The decision could affect numerous individuals across the country who use marijuana legally under state law but remain subject to federal gun restrictions.

The full implications of this ruling will become clearer as the court issues its complete written opinion and lower courts apply the precedent in future cases. The decision addresses a growing tension in American law as state-level marijuana reforms continue expanding while federal prohibitions remain in place.

This case represents a notable moment in the evolution of gun rights jurisprudence. It shows the court willing to strike down federal restrictions on firearm ownership even when tied to drug policy concerns. The ruling underscores how changing social attitudes and state laws around marijuana are forcing reconsideration of longstanding federal restrictions that were established when marijuana prohibitions faced virtually no state-level challenge.

cards.headline: Vance defends Trump Iran deal as oil flows through Strait of Hormuz
cards.teaser: The vice president said the memorandum of understanding is producing results as oil prices decline.
cards.body:
Vice President JD Vance defended President Trump's 14-point memorandum of understanding with Iran as a "win-win" for the United States. He highlighted that oil is now flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and prices are declining following the agreement.

Vance stated that if Iran fails to change its behavior regarding its military and nuclear programs, consequences will follow. When asked whether he feared Trump would blame him if the deal fails, Vance said he had no such concerns. Some Republican lawmakers, including Senator Ted Cruz, have criticized the agreement, though Senator Lindsey Graham softened his stance after discussions with Trump's special envoy.

cards.headline: White House sends Iran agreement to Congress
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers said they should have received the memorandum of understanding earlier.
cards.body:
The White House delivered the Iran memorandum of understanding to Congress. Some Republican lawmakers voiced complaints about the timing, saying they did not receive the agreement sooner than they did.

The delivery follows President Trump's negotiation of the memorandum with Iran. Vice President Vance has publicly defended the deal, saying oil is now moving through the Strait of Hormuz and prices are declining as a result of the agreement.

cards.headline: Senate committee advances bipartisan college sports regulation bill
cards.teaser: The Protect College Sports Act passed 19-9 and moves to the full Senate.
cards.body:
The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee advanced the Protect College Sports Act in a 19-9 vote, sending the bipartisan measure to regulate college sports to the Senate floor. Twelve Republicans and seven Democrats supported the bill, while seven Democrats and two Republicans opposed it.

Sens. Roger Wicker of Mississippi and others voted against the measure. The bill seeks to establish federal regulations for college athletics. The committee's approval marks a step toward potential nationwide standards for collegiate sports governance.

cards.headline: Trump administration removes dozens of exhibits from national parks
cards.teaser: Signs, exhibits and films were taken down as part of an effort to remove materials the administration says disparage Americans.
cards.body:
The Trump administration removed dozens of materials from at least 37 National Park Service sites, according to a new court filing. The items included signs, exhibits and films that the administration said disparage Americans.

The descriptions of what was removed remain vague in the court filing. The removals were part of a broader administration effort to purge content from national parks that officials deemed negative toward Americans. The National Park Service carried out the removals across multiple locations.

cards.headline: Sen. Van Hollen considers 2028 presidential run
cards.teaser: The Maryland Democrat said he is kicking the tires on a possible White House bid.
cards.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said he is "kicking the tires" on a possible 2028 presidential bid. The Democrat made the remarks during an interview on NOTUS's On NOTUS podcast as he has increasingly stepped into the political spotlight during President Trump's second term.

Van Hollen has raised his national profile in recent months as a vocal critic of the Trump administration.

cards.headline: Federal offices and services close for Juneteenth
cards.teaser: The federal holiday means some government services will be unavailable.
cards.body:
Federal offices and some services will be closed in observance of Juneteenth. The holiday commemorates the end of slavery in the United States.

Those planning errands involving federal agencies or services should expect closures. Juneteenth became a federal holiday in recent years, leading to annual closures of government offices on the observance date.
